newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Populist NZ leader says could swing right or left.
newsitem.headline: Populist NZ leader says could swing right or left.

text.p: Populist New Zealand First leader Winston Peters kept the country guessing on Tuesday by offering equal odds on a coalition deal with the right or left.

The charismatic Maori politician, breaking virtual silence since Saturday's inconclusive election, said the chances of teaming up with the conservative National Party or centre-left Labour were about even.
He said his party would negotiate with both sides, and it would not necessarily be harmful if the process dragged on until Christmas. "It's better to take time to get it right," he said.

National, in power since 1990, won 53 seats together with its allies and remains in power as a caretaker government until a new coalition is formed. Labour and the left-wing Alliance won a total of 50 seats.
Both the main parties have declared their aim of forming a government with support from New Zealand First's 17 MPs. Peters has said he expects a "bidding war" over policy.
The new parliament is due to meet by December 13. If no stable government can be formed, new elections would eventually be required.
Peters said he would be negotiating with National and Labour at about the same time in what he called a "dual negotiating process". He expected talks to start next week.
"We are ready to go," Peters said.

"We have a political system, a new one, and we intend and are determined to make it work. We want to secure an outcome that builds a strong export-led economy and addresses the outstanding social problems that are effecting New Zealand."

He said his priorities would be to uplift the underclass, give every child the education and healthcare needed to prepare them for life, treat the elderly fairly and attack a crisis in the mental health system.
New Zealand First won 13 percent of the vote at the election, but was drawing 30 percent in February after promising to cut immigration to the bone. Peters has denied targeting Asian immigrants.
Asked what message he had for Asians concerned about his party's position, Peters said they should examine the immigration policies of Asian countries.
"If they find a more liberal one than New Zealand's, let me know what it is," he said.
Peters pleaded for patience and calm from the financial markets, but said the New Zealand currency was too high for an export-led recovery -- a comment which immediately provoked a sell-down.
He criticised the central bank policies of both National and Labour and said the current inflation target of zero to two percent was no longer "respectable".
Peters has a long history of antagonism with Prime Minister Jim Bolger, who sacked him from National's cabinet in 1991, but has promised not to let personalities get in the way.
During the election campaign, however, Peters had supported his deputy Tau Henare when he ruled out working with Bolger and other senior members of the National cabinet.
